messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The afternoon sun had just hit the linoleum of the third-floor hallway when Daniel, the school counselor, stepped between two escalating teenagers. He misjudged the slickness from the morning mopping, his grip on the larger student’s jacket slipping as he tried to anchor him. The boy pitched forward, tumbled down the stairwell, and struck his head on the concrete landing with a sickening crack. In the months that followed, the accident did not settle into a distant report; instead, it replayed with full sensory reliving, each fragment feeling as present and unedited as the day it occurred. Daniel knew the facts of what happened, yet he consistently found himself unable to find words to describe the moment to anyone. When the school nurse’s clipboard clicked in the staff lounge or a supervisor’s voice grew tight with administrative stress, the hallway instantly replayed in his mind with perfect, unbroken clarity. Those environmental cues did not merely spark a flashback; they cemented his conviction that he was fundamentally unreliable and entirely at fault. Because he was certain he could never trust himself again, ordinary workplace demands morphed into imminent warnings, drawing his attention like a magnet to the disaster. The more vividly the past assaulted him, the more hyperaware he became, turning every routine medical check-up or staff meeting into a potential reminder. The visceral weight of those sensory intrusions constantly whispered that he was dangerous and had irrevocably shattered his future. His self-blame and life-destroyed beliefs made the fragmented moments of the accident feel less like a report and more like a live broadcast he could not pause. Convinced that his own judgment was poison, he systematically sidestepped any police or administrative review and buried himself in endless paperwork to avoid the possibility of error. His compulsive mental distraction only prevented the event from being processed as a completed memory, trapping it as an unending present. By running from his thoughts and shutting out officials, he interpreted his own coping mechanisms as proof that his life was truly ruined and his professional identity was gone. The habits he relied on to survive the weeks after the accident prevented his nervous system from habituating, leaving every subsequent smell or stressor feeling as sudden and catastrophic as the first. Maintaining that exhausting perimeter of avoidance and mental noise ensured his baseline anxiety never dropped, keeping his body permanently braced for another catastrophe. This relentless physical reactivity and exhausted sleep vigilance forced him to keep his attention perpetually occupied, as resting his mind felt synonymous with losing control. Whenever he finally lowered his guard in the quiet of his marital home, his heart would hammer against his ribs and a wave of crushing guilt and horror washed over him, leaving his muscles locked in cold dread. The constant state of high alert did not fade into the background; instead, it sharpened the edges of the recollection, pulling him back into the moment with increasing frequency. Even the faint scent of antiseptic from the staff clinic now triggered the same paralyzing fear, immediately pushing him to withdraw into frantic busywork to keep the panic at bay. Daniel’s wife finally called a therapist after he missed their daughter’s recital because he had spent the entire afternoon in his car, parked three blocks away, gripping the steering wheel to stop his hands from shaking. He arrived at the intake office with a PCL-5 score that reflected profound distress, hoping someone could help him untangle the knot in his chest. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the terrifying certainty that he would never be allowed to do the right thing again. He left the first session with a fragile hope that he might finally learn how to stop running from the past, even as he braced for the possibility that some fractures simply cannot be repaired.
